assessmentSummary.identity: A bilateral step-off from an individualized low platform into a short-contact bounce strategy, immediate maximal vertical rebound, and controlled bilateral final landing.
currentCardFindings: The card correctly describes a short-contact vertical rebound but provides no platform-height rule, contact-time target, final landing, or readiness criteria.
The 10-point absolute-load value and 50-point generic difficulty omit high impact, supervision, and consequence of error.
The active Drop Jump Reactive and several depth-drop rebound cards describe the same contact sequence and strategy.

proposedDosage.progressWhen: contact and rebound metrics remain inside the preset quality band with aligned contacts and controlled final landings

coachCues: Meet the floor stiff but not locked
athleteInstructions: Step from the box without jumping
Spend as little useful time on the floor as possible and rebound straight up

readiness: repeatable low hurdle or pogo rebound

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Use Drop Jump as the stable short-contact bounce identity. Consolidate Drop Jump Reactive and the low-box or depth-drop vertical rebound duplicates after human review; keep countermovement Depth Jump as a distinct strategy variant.

currentCardSnapshot.description: The athlete steps off a low box, contacts the ground briefly, and jumps vertically with minimal ground time.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effect of drop jump technique on the reactive strength index
claims: A platform step-off identity must specify whether the first ground contact ends in a held landing or an immediate rebound, and a rebound must specify bounce versus countermovement strategy, direction, contact-time intent, final landing, and reset.

Drop Jump must not combine landing-only depth drops, short-contact bounce drop jumps, deeper countermovement depth jumps, horizontal or lateral rebounds, repeated contacts, box-to-box sequences, or unilateral contacts.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of Plyometric Jump Training on the Reactive Strength Index in Healthy Individuals Across the Lifespan: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis
claims: Reactive strength describes producing a powerful concentric action immediately after an impact-induced eccentric action within the stretch-shortening cycle.

Drop Jump belongs to either landing absorption or reactive vertical power; platform height, ground-contact strategy, rebound direction, laterality, and final stabilization must remain controlled dimensions.

evidence.sourceTitle: Basics of Strength and Conditioning Manual
claims: Step-off landing and rebound coordinate the foot and ankle, knee, hip, pelvis, and trunk under rapid eccentric loading.

The card should assign plantar-flexor complex and intrinsic-foot roles, quadriceps and hip-extensor braking and propulsion, hamstring and frontal-plane hip stabilization, and trunk control without claiming one isolated tissue absorbs the drop.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effect of drop jump technique on the reactive strength index
claims: Bounce drop jumps produced shorter contact times but lower rebound height than countermovement drop jumps in the studied youth basketball players.

Observable technique must therefore match intent: a bounce strategy limits flexion and prioritizes short contact, while a countermovement strategy allows greater center-of-mass displacement and prioritizes rebound height without pausing.

evidence.sourceTitle: Methodological considerations for determining the volume and intensity of drop jump training. A systematic, critical and prepositive review
claims: Drop height alone is not an adequate intensity determinant; ground reaction force, power output, jump height, strategy, and individual readiness also matter.

Exercise difficulty must score technical and physical demand, coordination, supervision, consequence of error, impact, work-capacity demand, and overall difficulty directly; exercise cards must not use skill-library levels.

evidence.sourceTitle: Methodological considerations for determining the volume and intensity of drop jump training. A systematic, critical and prepositive review
claims: Drop-jump exposure depends on platform height, body mass, contact strategy, ground reaction force, output, surface, contacts, and recovery rather than platform height alone.
Drop Jump needs drop and landing contacts, impact and eccentric stress, target contact or rebound metric, technical-fatigue criteria, inter-repetition reset, and recovery guidance.

evidence.sourceTitle: Training interventions to reduce the risk of injury to the lower extremity joints during landing movements in adult athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
claims: Landing interventions depend on suitable materials, coaching knowledge, usable space, and task-specific progression.

The delivery profile should require a stable non-slip platform, unobstructed step-off edge, level landing surface, safe return route, adequate ceiling and spacing, athlete-specific drop height, and coach sightlines to both lower limbs.

evidence.sourceTitle: Methodological considerations for determining the volume and intensity of drop jump training. A systematic, critical and prepositive review
claims: Drop-jump programming requires explicit volume, intensity, recovery, surface, height-selection, and individualization criteria.

Prescribe discrete repetitions, platform-height rule, contact strategy, target contact or rebound outcome, final landing, inter-repetition reset, set rest, and stop threshold; do not use conditioning-style work intervals.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Use of Augmented Information for Reducing Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk During Jump Landings: A Systematic Review
claims: Specific feedback can improve landing mechanics, while excessive cue volume can interfere with learning.

Use a small strategy-specific cue set: step off without jumping up, meet the floor evenly, either absorb and own the landing or reverse immediately, finish tall in the prescribed direction, and control the final landing.

evidence.sourceTitle: Basics of Strength and Conditioning Manual
claims: Depth and drop jumps impose advanced eccentric and reactive demands and require progression from lower-intensity landing and jumping tasks.

Stop for pain, giving way, apprehension, platform instability, asymmetrical contact, loud or collapsed landing, valgus, heel whip, trunk loss, unintended pause, missed strategy, slower contact, lower rebound, or uncontrolled final landing.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of Plyometric Jump Training on the Reactive Strength Index in Healthy Individuals Across the Lifespan: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis
claims: Plyometric jump training can improve reactive strength, but effects and readiness differ across populations and training contexts.

Drop Jump belongs early in a fresh output block after the athlete owns landing absorption and lower-intensity rebounds; dose and height should be individualized and volume should end before contact or output quality declines.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Use of Augmented Information for Reducing Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk During Jump Landings: A Systematic Review
claims: Athlete support should show the platform, step-off direction, first contact, intended flexion strategy, rebound vector, final landing, and the one metric that defines success.
The interface should distinguish 'fast off the floor' from 'jump as high as possible' and explain that a higher platform is not automatically a better or harder prescription.

evidence.sourceTitle: Methodological considerations for determining the volume and intensity of drop jump training. A systematic, critical and prepositive review
claims: Coach support should individualize drop height and record contacts, surface, technique, output, and recovery rather than relying on a generic height progression.

Provide front and side observation, bounce-versus-countermovement criteria, contact-time and rebound-height options, left-right comparison, height-reduction rules, regressions, progressions, and final-landing gates.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Plyometric selection and progression should match physical and psychosocial readiness, technical competence, supervision, and equipment scale.

Accessibility can be improved with a lower step, landing-only depth drop, assisted step-down, visual landing marks, quieter environment, longer reset, or floor rebound regression without assigning an exercise skill level.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effect of drop jump technique on the reactive strength index
claims: Bounce and countermovement drop-jump techniques produce materially different contact-time and rebound-height outcomes.

Platform height and submaximal intent are delivery modifiers; changing landing-only versus rebound intent, bounce versus countermovement strategy, rebound vector, laterality, obstacle sequence, or repeated contacts requires a controlled variant or distinct definition.

alternateAssessments.name: Drop Jump Reactive
alternateAssessments.rationale: Reactive is inherent to the short-contact drop-jump identity.

alternateAssessments.name: Countermovement Depth Jump
alternateAssessments.rationale: A deeper countermovement prioritizes rebound height and lengthens contact.

alternateAssessments.name: Depth Drop to Stick
alternateAssessments.rationale: A held first landing removes the rebound.

alternateAssessments.name: Drop Jump to Broad Rebound
alternateAssessments.rationale: Horizontal rebound changes projection and braking.

alternateAssessments.name: Repeated Drop Jumps
alternateAssessments.rationale: Multiple rebounds change contact count, fatigue, and logistics.
